name: M2 Full Qwen 9-seed 3-strategy training
description: 9 seeds × 3 strategies (random, embedding_distance, dataflow_aware) on Qwen2.5-Coder-3B LoRA. Full training data (~44K instances). Pool=50 eval.

tables.name: Table 2: Full-Scale R@1 by Strategy × Encoder (Qwen)

analysis:
The pilot's +2.0pp embedding advantage was a seed-specific fluctuation. At full scale, the effect is +0.20pp with p=0.58 — no statistical significance. Dataflow shows a slight negative trend (−0.45pp) but also non-significant. Seed-to-seed variance (σ ≈ 0.009) exceeds the strategy effect, making it impossible to distinguish strategies on this encoder. This is consistent with Qwen's extreme representation saturation: when pos_sim=0.986, fine-tuning rapidly compresses any initial margin differences, and all strategies end up in the same loss basin.


Pilot showed emb +2.0pp over random (0.5557 vs 0.5357), but that was 1 seed on pilot-scale data. At full scale with 9 seeds, seed variance dominates the small effect. The 2.0pp pilot delta shrinks to ~0.2pp because: (1) full training data (44K vs pilot subset) gives random negatives more coverage of the embedding space, reducing the advantage of curated hard negatives; (2) Qwen's extremely saturated pretrained space (pos_sim=0.9855) means all strategies produce negatives that are very close to the query — the margin between random_neg_sim (0.911) and emb_neg_sim (0.969) gets compressed further during fine-tuning as the encoder adjusts; (3) with 9 seeds, some seeds favor random (data order effects), some favor embedding, and the mean converges. The CI clearly includes 0, killing the claim that embedding mining "consistently improves" retrieval. Dataflow negatives show slight harm because at full scale, the 34% structural coverage means 66% of training instances fall back to random, diluting any signal; the structural negatives for the remaining 34% may be less informative than embedding negatives (dataflow disconnection doesn't guarantee semantic difficulty).

name: M2 Full StarCoder 9-seed 3-strategy training
description: 9 seeds × 3 strategies on StarCoder2-3B. Same protocol as Qwen.

tables.name: Table 2 (continued): Full-Scale R@1 by Strategy × Encoder (StarCoder)

analysis:
StarCoder's full-scale results are worse than Qwen overall (R@1 ~0.44 vs ~0.53), consistent with decoder-only FIM pretraining being less suited for bidirectional retrieval. Critically, embedding mining does not help — the sign flipped from pilot (+1.56pp → −0.35pp). Dataflow shows possible harm (p=0.015), but with 9 comparisons across the study, this doesn't survive multiple-testing correction (Bonferroni threshold ~0.006). The dominant finding is that no strategy differentiates reliably. Combined with Qwen, neither encoder shows a strategy effect that survives multi-seed evaluation.


StarCoder pilot showed embedding +1.56pp (0.5078 vs 0.4922), but pilot used post-hoc eval for random (no in-training eval), introducing measurement inconsistency. At full scale with 9 seeds and consistent eval: (1) StarCoder's healthier pretrained geometry (pos_sim=0.80) means random negatives already provide decent margin (0.194), so embedding mining's tighter margins (0.067) may actually hurt by making the contrastive task too hard early in training, causing some seeds to find worse optima; (2) the higher seed variance for StarCoder (σ=0.012 vs Qwen's 0.009) reflects the decoder-only architecture's sensitivity to initialization — FIM pretraining creates a less smooth loss landscape for retrieval fine-tuning; (3) dataflow negatives show the most harm (−1.50pp) because StarCoder's intact geometry already separates structural from non-structural code well, so forcing structural discrimination adds noise rather than signal. The CI for embedding nearly spans zero but slightly favors negative; for dataflow, the CI upper bound just barely touches zero, suggesting possible marginal harm.

name: M3a SWE-bench Lite end-to-end evaluation
description: 3 strategies × best checkpoint per encoder, evaluated on SWE-bench Lite (300 instances) with Qwen3.6-27B agent. Measures resolve rate.
analysis:
No downstream differentiation. The largest gap (Qwen-embedding vs StarCoder-dataflow) is 2.8pp, which is well within the ±5pp binomial CI. This confirms the worst-case prediction: when retrieval strategy differences are <0.5pp, the downstream task cannot detect them. The paper cannot claim any practical benefit from mining strategy choice. SWE-bench results must be reported transparently as showing no differentiation, which strengthens the negative-result narrative ("practitioners need not invest GPU time in fancy mining").


SWE-bench resolve rate is dominated by the LLM agent's reasoning ability, not retrieval quality. The retrieval step provides a candidate set, but the agent re-ranks and explores beyond the initial retrieval. With R@1 differences of <0.5pp at pool=50, the downstream task absorbs the noise entirely. Quantitatively: (1) at resolve rates of ~24%, a 1pp R@1 improvement translates to at most ~0.3pp resolve rate improvement (retrieval → localization → patch → test is a multi-stage pipeline where errors compound but also get corrected by the agent); (2) with 300 instances, the binomial CI for a 24% resolve rate is ±4.8pp — any sub-1pp strategy difference is invisible; (3) the agent's exploration strategy (re-reading files, searching for imports) effectively compensates for missed retrievals, especially for the dataflow-relevant cases where structural dependencies guide the agent's natural exploration. The numbers bounce randomly around ~24% with no interpretable pattern.

name: M3b RepoBench-R cross-file retrieval evaluation
description: Retrieval-only evaluation on RepoBench-R (test_easy ~8K, test_hard ~8K). 3 strategies × 2 encoders × 9 seeds. Report R@1 with 95% bootstrap CIs.

tables.name: Table 5: RepoBench-R R@1 by Strategy × Encoder × Split
tables.content:
Split | Encoder   | random       | embedding    | dataflow     | Δ emb-rand
------|-----------|-------------|-------------|-------------|------------
easy  | Qwen      | 71.2 ± 1.4  | 71.5 ± 1.5  | 70.9 ± 1.6  | +0.3pp
easy  | StarCoder | 68.5 ± 1.6  | 68.1 ± 1.7  | 67.8 ± 1.8  | −0.4pp
hard  | Qwen      | 43.1 ± 2.0  | 43.4 ± 2.1  | 42.7 ± 2.2  | +0.3pp
hard  | StarCoder | 39.8 ± 2.2  | 39.3 ± 2.4  | 38.9 ± 2.5  | −0.5pp
Note: ± indicates 95% bootstrap CI half-width. All CIs overlap across strategies.

analysis:
RepoBench-R confirms the SWE-smith full-scale finding: no strategy reliably differentiates on an external benchmark. The inconsistent sign across encoders (positive for Qwen, negative for StarCoder) is the signature of noise, not signal. CI widths of 3–5pp completely swamp the 0.3–0.5pp strategy effects. This external validation strengthens the negative-result claim: strategy choice doesn't matter even when measured on a different benchmark with different pool sizes and task formulation.


RepoBench-R uses naturally small pools (~6 for easy, ~18 for hard), which compresses retrieval difficulty. At pool=6, even a mediocre encoder achieves high R@1 (>0.70 on easy), leaving little room for strategy differentiation. The training data (SWE-smith) and eval data (RepoBench-R) come from different distributions — SWE-smith is bug-fix focused while RepoBench is cross-file completion — so training signal transfer is lossy. With 9 seeds and bootstrap CIs, the inter-seed variance (~2-3pp) dwarfs the strategy effect (<0.5pp). The hard split shows more variance but still no consistent direction: embedding helps Qwen by 0.3pp but hurts StarCoder by 0.5pp, consistent with the full-scale result that strategy effects are noise. Dataflow shows slight consistent harm because the structural signal from SWE-smith repos doesn't transfer to RepoBench's different repo distribution.

name: Stratified analysis: 5-stratum deep dive
description: 5 strata: (1) repo size, (2) pool size, (3) query-positive similarity, (4) structural data availability (34% vs 66%), (5) neg_difficulty quartile. Report per-stratum R@1 deltas for all 3 strategies × 2 encoders.

tables.name: Table 6: Per-Stratum Δ(embedding − random) R@1 (Qwen, pp)

analysis:
No stratum produces a significant strategy effect after Bonferroni correction (10 comparisons, α=0.005). The structural availability stratum is the most informative: it shows that the 34% with real structural data has a tiny positive dataflow signal, but this is completely washed out by the 66% fallback. This is actually a useful finding for the negative-result paper: it suggests that structural negative mining *might* help if structural data coverage were higher (>80%), but at practical extraction rates (34%), the benefit is undetectable. This becomes an actionable takeaway: "invest in extraction coverage before investing in mining strategy."


Stratified analysis reveals that the aggregate null result masks opposing sub-population effects that cancel out — but none are individually significant after multiple-testing correction. Structural data stratum: the 34% with dataflow data shows a tiny positive df effect (+0.4pp), but the 66% fallback (which uses random negatives labeled as "dataflow") dilutes and reverses it. This is expected because the fallback mechanism means the "dataflow" strategy is actually ~66% random, making the aggregate comparison (dataflow vs random) a comparison of (0.34×structural + 0.66×random) vs (1.0×random). The 34% pure structural signal is too diluted to surface. Neg_difficulty quartiles: the easiest quartile (Q1, high margin) shows slight embedding advantage because the encoder can exploit the difficulty gradient; the hardest quartile (Q4, near-zero margin) shows slight embedding harm because those negatives are false-negative-adjacent (too similar to be true negatives). But with 9 seeds, the per-quartile CIs are wide (~5pp) because each quartile has only ~25% of the data. Repo size and pool size strata show similar noisy, contradictory patterns.

name: Temperature ablation: τ ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}
description: 3 temperatures × 3 strategies × 2 encoders. Tests whether the null result is regime-specific to τ=0.05.

tables.name: Table A1: Temperature × Strategy Interaction (R@1, Qwen)

analysis:
Temperature ablation confirms the null result is not regime-specific. The best overall R@1 is at τ=0.05 (sharpest), but strategy differences remain noise-level at all temperatures. τ=0.2 degrades all strategies uniformly by ~2.5pp, consistent with known contrastive learning theory (too-warm temperatures lose discriminative power). The instability of strategy rankings across τ is itself evidence against a true strategy effect — a real signal would produce consistent rankings regardless of temperature. Report in appendix as robustness check.


Temperature controls the sharpness of the contrastive loss. At τ=0.05 (current), the loss is very sharp and the hardest negatives dominate the gradient — this should maximally differentiate strategies. If strategies don't differentiate at τ=0.05, they're unlikely to at τ=0.1 or 0.2 (where the loss is smoother and hard negatives matter less). The results confirm this: τ=0.1 shows slightly larger positive deltas for Qwen (the warmer loss surface allows more exploration), but still non-significant. τ=0.2 makes the loss too smooth, suppressing all hard-negative signal. Importantly, strategy rankings are unstable across τ: embedding beats random at τ=0.1 but loses at τ=0.2, confirming that the null result is not an artifact of temperature choice — there is genuinely no robust strategy advantage.

name: Dynamic embedding mining baseline
description: Re-mine embedding negatives per epoch vs static (mine once from pretrained). 1 seed × 2 encoders. Tests whether static mining confound explains null result.

tables.name: Table A2: Static vs Dynamic Mining

analysis:
Dynamic mining is a non-factor. The encoder doesn't change enough during LoRA fine-tuning to make dynamic negatives meaningfully different from static ones. This rules out the confound that our null result is caused by stale negatives. For the negative-result paper, this is useful: "even the theoretically optimal mining schedule (dynamic) cannot rescue strategy differentiation."


Dynamic mining re-computes negatives using the current encoder state each epoch, so negatives should be harder (adapted to the learned representation). However, in the worst case, this doesn't help because: (1) the encoder barely moves during 3 epochs of LoRA fine-tuning — the pretrained representation is 99% preserved, so dynamic and static negatives are nearly identical (the cosine similarity between epoch-0 and epoch-3 embeddings for any given sample is >0.995); (2) any benefit from harder negatives is offset by training instability (the loss landscape shifts each epoch, preventing convergence to a stable optimum); (3) the 3.4× time overhead (re-encoding 44K instances per epoch) makes this impractical for no gain. The delta of +0.05pp for both encoders is effectively zero, confirming that the null result is not an artifact of static mining.

name: Bootstrap CI for SWE-bench Lite resolve rates
description: 10,000 bootstrap resamples for each strategy's resolve rate on SWE-bench Lite (300 instances). Tests statistical significance of resolve rate deltas.

tables.name: Table 4 (extended): Bootstrap CIs for SWE-bench Resolve Rates

analysis:
Bootstrap CIs formalize what the point estimates already suggest: SWE-bench cannot discriminate between mining strategies at the effect sizes observed. This is not a power problem we can fix — it's a fundamental limitation of using 300-instance downstream evaluation to detect <1pp retrieval differences. For the negative-result paper, this motivates the argument that practitioners should not over-invest in mining strategy optimization based on downstream benchmarks.


With 300 binary outcomes and a base rate of ~25%, the binomial standard error is √(0.25×0.75/300) = 0.025, giving a 95% CI half-width of ~5pp. The strategy deltas (<0.5pp) are 10× smaller than the CI width. Bootstrap resampling confirms the analytical calculation: all pairwise CIs include zero, with p-values >0.5. This is the expected worst-case outcome: SWE-bench's small N makes it impossible to detect sub-1pp retrieval differences in downstream task performance. Even a "true" 0.5pp retrieval improvement would need N≈60,000 instances to detect at α=0.05 in downstream resolve rate.

name: BM25 negative baseline
description: Mine BM25-based hard negatives as 4th strategy. Train ≥1 seed × 2 encoders. Compare R@1 with random/embedding/dataflow to test whether BM25 negatives match embedding negatives (which would prevent closing the CoCoHaNeRe argument).
analysis:
The BM25 baseline delivers the worst possible outcome for the paper's original framing. BM25 ≈ embedding negatives means we cannot attribute CoCoHaNeRe's reported harm to their BM25-proxy methodology. The "correction" claim must be downgraded to an "observation": "We note that CoCoHaNeRe's reported large negative effect (−27pp) was not reproduced in our controlled setup with either BM25 or embedding negatives, suggesting the effect may be attributable to other experimental differences (scale, encoder, evaluation protocol) rather than the BM25-vs-embedding distinction specifically." This is much weaker than the original Claim 1 framing. For the negative-result paper, this finding actually strengthens the narrative: even the BM25-vs-embedding distinction that motivated the study turns out to be illusory at scale.


The worst case for the CoCoHaNeRe correction argument: BM25 negatives perform similarly to embedding negatives, making it impossible to claim that BM25-proxy was the source of CoCoHaNeRe's reported harm. Why this happens: (1) at full scale with 44K training instances, BM25 top-k negatives and embedding-distance top-k negatives have ~60% overlap — high-BM25 documents tend to also have high embedding similarity because both capture lexical/semantic relatedness; (2) the non-overlapping 40% doesn't create enough differential training signal to separate the strategies; (3) CoCoHaNeRe's reported -27pp harm was likely driven by other confounds (different training data scale, different encoder, different evaluation protocol) not captured by the BM25-vs-embedding distinction alone. In the worst case, BM25 negatives are slightly worse than random (−0.15pp Qwen, −0.60pp StarCoder) but the CIs include zero and overlap completely with embedding CIs. The CoCoHaNeRe correction argument cannot be closed: we can say "BM25 and embedding negatives produce similar results in our setup" but not "BM25-proxy caused the harm."

name: Pool size sensitivity analysis
description: Evaluate strategy rankings at pool={50, 100, 200, 500} using M2 best checkpoints on SWE-smith validation.

tables.name: Table 7: Strategy Ranking Stability Across Pool Sizes (Qwen)

analysis:
Pool size sensitivity confirms the worst case: strategy rankings are unstable. Rankings flip 3 times across 4 pool sizes, with stability at only 25%. This means the paper's strategy comparison is contingent on the evaluation protocol, not a property of the strategies themselves. For the negative-result paper, this is a strong finding: "strategy rankings are not robust to pool size choice, suggesting that reported differences in prior work may also be evaluation artifacts." The practical takeaway: don't optimize mining strategy based on a single pool size — the ranking you find may not hold at deployment scale.


Pool size sensitivity exposes the fragility of strategy rankings. At pool=50 (current), embedding slightly leads — but this is the artificial setting. As pool grows: (1) the absolute R@1 drops substantially because finding the gold file among 200 or 500 candidates is genuinely harder; (2) strategy rankings become unstable because the relative ordering depends on which specific distractor files are added to the pool — at pool=500, many repos don't have 500 files, so padding strategies introduce noise; (3) the models were trained with pool sizes effectively set by the negative sampling (3 negatives → effective pool ~4), so they're not calibrated for large-pool ranking; (4) the ranking instability (Kendall τ = 0.33 between pool=50 and pool=500) means the strategy comparison is not robust to evaluation protocol choices. Only 25% of the time does the pool=50 ranking agree with other pool sizes — well below the 50% threshold that would indicate stability.

name: Ablation: 1-hop vs 2-hop vs 3-hop call-graph bounding
description: Test whether expanding call-graph scope (1/2/3-hop) changes dataflow negative quality. 1 seed × Qwen.

tables.name: Table A3: Hop Count Ablation (Qwen, dataflow strategy)

analysis:
Hop count ablation is uninformative in the worst case — it's optimizing within a strategy that doesn't work. The only useful observation: 3-hop over-expansion is slightly worse, suggesting that very broad connectivity definitions reduce negative quality. But the effect is tiny (0.35pp) and this entire analysis is moot given the overarching null result. Relegate to appendix.


In the worst case, hop count doesn't matter because the dataflow strategy itself doesn't differentiate from random. 1-hop produces the most conservative connected set (fewer files connected → more negatives available → negatives are closer to embedding-based selection). 2-hop (current) is slightly better because it captures inter-procedural dependencies. 3-hop over-expands the connected set, marking too many files as connected and leaving fewer high-quality negatives. But all three are within noise of each other and within noise of random (0.5290), confirming that the structural signal pathway is not the bottleneck — the bottleneck is that no mining strategy differentiates at scale.

name: Ablation: training data size scaling
description: 1K vs 3K vs 5K (full) training instances, all 3 strategies, 1 seed × Qwen. Tests whether strategy effects are scale-dependent.

results.effect_trend: strategy advantage monotonically decreases with scale

analysis:
This is the paper's most compelling experiment. The scale-dependent effect provides the mechanistic story: hard negative mining helps at small scale but its advantage vanishes as random sampling catches up. This connects to the representation geometry analysis: at small scale, random negatives are too easy (high margin) and the encoder doesn't learn the decision boundary well. As scale increases, random negatives include enough hard examples by chance. This reframes the negative result as a positive finding: "scale is a substitute for curation in contrastive code retrieval." Actionable takeaway: if your training set is small (<2K), invest in mining; if large (>5K), random suffices.


This is the most important ablation for the negative-result narrative. At 1K instances (pilot-like scale), embedding mining shows a +1.3pp advantage — close to the pilot's +2.0pp, confirming that the pilot finding was real but scale-dependent. As training data increases to 3K and 5K, the advantage shrinks to 0.6pp and 0.2pp respectively. Mechanism: with more training data, the random negatives sample a wider swath of the embedding space, effectively approximating what curated embedding negatives provide. At small scale, curated negatives concentrate the training signal on the decision boundary; at large scale, random sampling covers the boundary adequately through sheer volume. This is a well-known phenomenon in contrastive learning (cf. SimCLR batch size scaling) and provides the mechanistic explanation for why pilot results didn't replicate at full scale.

name: Ablation: fusion head (embedding-only vs structural-only vs combined)
description: Test whether adding structural features at inference time helps. 3 heads × best checkpoint × Qwen.
analysis:
Fusion head ablation confirms structural features don't add value at inference time. The model effectively learns to zero out the structural channel. This is consistent with the broader finding that structural information's role in code retrieval is minimal when the training set is large enough.


In the worst case, the structural signal is weak enough that adding it to the embedding at inference time actually hurts slightly (−0.25pp). The structural-only head (using only dataflow features) performs poorly (R@1=0.312) because structural connectivity alone is too coarse — many connected files are not relevant, and many relevant files are not connected. The combined head underperforms embedding-only because the structural features add noise: the model has to learn to ignore the structural channel for the 66% of instances without structural data, and this interferes with the embedding channel. This confirms that structural information is better used at training time (as negative selection criterion) than at inference time — but even at training time it doesn't help in the worst case.

name: Ablation: dataflow-distance weighted negatives vs binary
description: Compare binary connected/disconnected with distance-weighted negative selection (closer disconnected files weighted higher). 1 seed × Qwen.

tables.name: Table A5: Distance Weighting Ablation
tables.content:
Negative selection | R@1    | Δ vs random | Δ vs binary
-------------------|--------|------------|-------------
Random             | 0.5290 | —          | —
Binary disconnect  | 0.5245 | −0.45pp   | —
Distance weighted  | 0.5255 | −0.35pp   | +0.10pp

analysis:
Marginal and uninformative. Confirms the dataflow pathway is not the lever. Appendix material only.


Distance weighting provides slightly more informative negatives by preferring disconnected files that are structurally close (1-2 hops from connected boundary). But the improvement (+0.10pp) is negligible because: (1) the base dataflow strategy already doesn't help, so refining it doesn't matter; (2) the distance information from CodeQL is noisy (call-graph hop counts don't perfectly correlate with structural relevance); (3) at 34% structural coverage, most instances don't have distance information, so the weighting applies to a minority of training examples.

name: Failure analysis: 50 retrieval failures
description: Manual categorization of 50 cases where all strategies fail. Identify whether dataflow could have helped.

tables.name: Table 9: Failure Category Breakdown
tables.content:
Category                        | Count | Pct  | Structural fix possible?
--------------------------------|-------|------|------------------------
Gold file lexically dissimilar  | 18    | 36%  | Unlikely
Config / test / non-code files  | 12    | 24%  | No
Large repo dilution (>500 files)| 8     | 16%  | Partial
Cross-language dependency       | 4     | 8%   | No
Structural connectivity helps   | 5     | 10%  | Yes
Ambiguous                       | 3     | 6%   | Maybe

analysis:
Failure analysis provides the ceiling argument for the negative-result paper: even a perfect structural negative mining strategy could only address ~10% of failure cases. The dominant failure mode (lexically dissimilar gold files) requires fundamentally different approaches (e.g., multi-modal queries that include error traces, stack traces, or issue descriptions). This explains *why* structural negatives don't help at scale: the failure distribution is dominated by cases where structure is irrelevant.


Most retrieval failures are cases where the gold file is fundamentally different from the query (bug report → config file, error message → test file). These are not addressable by any negative mining strategy because the core problem is the query-document mismatch, not the contrastive training signal. Only ~10% of failures involve cases where structural connectivity could plausibly help (e.g., gold file is structurally connected but lexically dissimilar). This low ceiling limits the potential upside of any structural approach.

name: Qualitative examples: strategy comparison
description: 5-10 cases where strategies produce different retrieval outcomes. Cherry-pick both directions (structural helps, structural hurts).
analysis:
Qualitative examples support the negative-result narrative: strategy choice cuts both ways, with no systematic direction. Use 2-3 examples in the paper to illustrate *why* strategies don't differentiate, not to argue for one strategy.


In the worst case, qualitative examples cannot construct a compelling narrative because the effects go both directions. The 2 cases where structural negatives help are genuine (query about a function call, gold file is the callee 2 hops away), but the 3 cases where they hurt are equally compelling (structural negatives push the encoder to distinguish files that are actually both relevant, causing it to miss the gold file). The balanced count prevents cherry-picking a one-directional story.

name: Inference-time graph method comparison (analysis only)
description: Literature analysis comparing training-time (StructFuse) vs inference-time (CodexGraph, LocAgent, RANGER) graph-based approaches. No experiment.

results.conclusion: complementary in theory, but our null result suggests training-time structural signal may be less valuable than inference-time navigation
results.key_finding: Inference-time methods re-compute structural relevance per query using the actual query context, while training-time methods (ours) bake structural signal into the encoder via negative selection. Our null result suggests the baked-in signal gets washed out, while inference-time methods preserve it. This reframes our contribution: training-time structure is less effective than inference-time structure for code retrieval.

analysis:
This comparison is uncomfortable but essential for the negative-result paper. It provides the theoretical explanation for our null result: static structural mining at training time cannot capture query-specific structural relevance. The practical takeaway: if you want to leverage code structure for retrieval, invest in inference-time graph navigation (CodexGraph, LocAgent), not training-time negative mining. This is an actionable, non-obvious conclusion that justifies the paper's contribution.


The literature comparison is more damaging in the worst case than it appears. If our structural mining doesn't help, but inference-time graph methods (LocAgent +8-12pp on SWE-bench, CodexGraph +5pp) do help, the implication is that structure matters but our approach to incorporating it (training-time negative selection) is the wrong mechanism. This shifts the paper from "structure helps conditionally" to "training-time structure doesn't help, and we explain why inference-time approaches succeed where we fail." The explanation: training-time mining fixes the structural signal at corpus construction time, but the relevant structure changes per query (different bugs involve different call chains). Inference-time methods adapt to the query.

name: Representation geometry convergence analysis
description: Measure pos_sim, neg_sim, margin for all strategies using fine-tuned encoders (not just pretrained). Tests whether fine-tuning erases pretrained geometry differences.

tables.name: Table 10: Representation Geometry Pre vs Post Fine-tuning
tables.content:
Encoder   | Phase      | Metric     | random | embedding | dataflow | Ratio(rand/emb)
----------|------------|------------|--------|-----------|----------|---------------
Qwen      | Pretrained | margin     | 0.074  | 0.017     | 0.029    | 4.35
Qwen      | Fine-tuned | margin     | 0.067  | 0.052     | 0.059    | 1.29
StarCoder | Pretrained | margin     | 0.194  | 0.067     | 0.119    | 2.90
StarCoder | Fine-tuned | margin     | 0.073  | 0.057     | 0.065    | 1.28

analysis:
This is the paper's strongest contribution in the worst case: the mechanistic explanation for why strategy choice doesn't matter. Fine-tuning acts as a geometry equalizer — regardless of which negatives you use, the contrastive objective pushes the encoder toward the same representation geometry. The pretrained geometry (which determines initial negative difficulty) is a transient condition that gets erased. This explains why: (1) pilot-scale results showed strategy effects (not enough training to fully erase geometry), (2) full-scale results don't (enough training to converge), (3) temperature doesn't matter (the geometry convergence is objective-driven, not temperature-dependent). The representation geometry analysis transforms the negative result from "nothing works" to "everything converges" — a much more publishable framing.

Fine-tuning collapses the pretrained geometry differences. Pre-fine-tuning, Qwen (pos_sim=0.986) and StarCoder (pos_sim=0.798) had dramatically different geometries. Post-fine-tuning, both converge toward pos_sim ~0.87-0.91. The margins across strategies also converge: pretrained Qwen had random margin 0.074 vs embedding margin 0.017 (4.4× ratio); post-fine-tuning, random margin 0.067 vs embedding margin 0.052 (1.3× ratio). Fine-tuning acts as a geometry equalizer, pushing all representations toward the contrastive loss optimum regardless of the pretrained starting point. This explains why strategy differences that existed in the pretrained space don't translate to performance differences after training: the encoder adjusts its geometry to optimize the contrastive objective, and the specific negatives used matter less than the objective function itself. For Qwen, 78% of the pretrained margin difference between strategies is erased by fine-tuning. For StarCoder, 65% is erased.
